raw_case_text: A 54-year-old gentleman with a history of well-controlled HIV established on Truvada and raltegravir, seizures, migraines, and previously treated syphilis presented to Croydon University Hospital with a 4-week history of progressive left leg weakness, bowel and bladder change, and a 1-week history of dysesthesia (Table 2). He denied any infective symptoms, weight loss, and personal or family history of tuberculosis (TB). He had no recent travel and reported no new sexual partners. Clinical examination revealed a normal cardiorespiratory examination. Neurologically, the patient had brisk reflexes in all limbs with reduced power (MRC 0/5) in the left leg combined with sensory dissociation starting from T5 in keeping with Brown-Sequard syndrome. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine undertaken at this time identified two peripherally enhancing cavitating lesions at T4-T5 with associated meningeal thickening and cord oedema. These images were felt indicative of CNS TB. Following this, anti-TB medication was started, and the patient was transferred to St. George's Hospital for further care. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis undertaken revealed highly elevated protein (3.07 g/L) and white cell count (7 x 109/L). CSF cryptococcal antigen (CRAG), TB molecular testing (GeneXpert), microscopy and culture, and viral polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were all negative. Serial sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB), peripheral blood cultures, and Q-interferon tests were negative. At this point, syphilis serological testing was undertaken; this suggested highly active acute infection (serum EIA positive and rapid plasma reagin (RPR) (1 in 64)). CSF serology showed positive Treponema pallidum particle agglutination (TPPA) 10240 and RPR 1 in 2 suggesting active disease. This raised the possibility of neurosyphilis with spinal syphilitic gumma. Due to no conclusive TB diagnosis, concurrent neurosyphilis treatment was initiated by way of 14-day high-dose benzylpenicillin therapy commencing on day 11 of presentation. Repeat MRI of the spine on days 12 and 22 of admission revealed incremental improvement in both spinal cord oedema and the size of the T4-T5 lesions (Figure 1). Following this, positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) scan was performed on day 41 which showed no significant areas of increased uptake outside of the spine for potential biopsy. This improvement in the spinal disease was associated with progressive and marked improvements in his neurology, and by day 55, the patient could walk several lengths of parallel bars from being previously bedbound.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 54-year-old man with well-controlled HIV presented with a 4-week history of progressive left lower extremity weakness and bowel/bladder dysfunction, and a 1-week history of truncal/limb dysesthesia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 4 weeks prior to presentation, the patient developed progressive left leg paralysis and sphincter disturbance followed 1 week prior by sensory dysesthesias below the upper thorax.
subjective.past_medical_history: Well-controlled HIV infection on emtricitabine/tenofovir (Truvada) and raltegravir; history of previously treated syphilis, seizures, and migraines. Denied recent travel, new sexual partners, or personal/family history of tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left leg weakness, sensory dissociation, and bowel/bladder dysfunction; negative for fever, weight loss, or respiratory symptoms. Home medications: Truvada and raltegravir.

objective.physical_examination: Normal cardiorespiratory exam. Neurological exam demonstrated a classic T5 Brown-Séquard syndrome: 0/5 MRC motor power in the left leg, brisk deep tendon reflexes in all four limbs, and dissociated sensory loss below the T5 dermatome.
objective.routine_investigations: Negative serial sputum AFB smears, peripheral blood cultures, and QuantiFERON-TB Gold assay. Serum syphilis testing was strongly positive (EIA positive, RPR 1:64).
objective.advanced_workup: Thoracic spine MRI identified two peripherally enhancing cavitating intramedullary/meningeal lesions at T4–T5 with focal pachymeningeal thickening and cord edema. Lumbar puncture CSF showed markedly elevated protein (3.07 g/L) and pleocytosis (WBC 7 × 10^9/L), with negative CSF cryptococcal antigen, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, AFB microscopy/culture, and viral PCR, whereas CSF syphilis serology was diagnostic of active neurosyphilis (CSF TPPA 1:10,240; CSF RPR 1:2). Day-41 whole-body PET-CT showed no extraspinal hypermetabolic lesions.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Although empirical anti-TB therapy was initially started for suspected intramedullary spinal tuberculomas, negative CSF GeneXpert, AFB cultures, and QuantiFERON alongside strongly reactive serum (RPR 1:64) and CSF (TPPA 1:10,240, RPR 1:2) treponemal/non-treponemal titers established thoracic spinal syphilitic gumma (meningovascular/gummatous neurosyphilis) causing Brown-Séquard syndrome. Treatment with a 14-day course of high-dose intravenous benzylpenicillin (commenced on day 11) produced rapid regression of the T4–T5 lesions and cord edema on day-12 and day-22 MRIs and restored ambulation by day 55.
